<description>
{
 "summary": "Releases inbound and manual peers from the initial headers synchronization slot when they reply to a getheaders request with an empty headers message while the chain tip is more than 24 hours old. It clears the peer's sync state and download deadline while setting a retry delay, allowing another eligible peer to take over headers synchronization. Automatic outbound connections remain unchanged, as they already handle stale peers via eviction and timeouts.",
 "problem": "During initial block download or when the best known header is more than a day old, a node queries only one peer for initial headers sync. If an inbound or manual peer (such as an addnode peer) is also syncing or caught up to the node's tip, it returns a valid empty headers message but remains designated as the active sync peer. Because inbound and manual peers are not subject to automatic outbound eviction and headers timeouts do not release the sync slot, initial sync can stall indefinitely even when other connected peers have the latest chain.",
 "evidence": [
  "Fixes issue #34096 ('IBD stalls if addnode peer is in IBD').",
  "Author provides a minimal reproducer demonstrating that with two inbound peers where the first returns empty headers, an unpatched node stalls for 10 seconds until the test timeout, whereas the patched node immediately falls back to the replacement peer."

<category name="p2p" title="P2P">
## Covers

Everything between this node and other nodes: connection management and
peer selection, address management, the message protocol and its
transport (including the encrypted v2 transport), block and transaction
relay including compact blocks, headers sync, transaction request and
orphan handling, network-level DoS protections, and the Tor, I2P, and
CJDNS integrations. The P2P and Private Broadcast labels are a strong
prior.

Not p2p: what the node does with a block or transaction once received
(validation, mempool); RPCs that merely report peer state (rpc).

## What matters here

Resistance to attack first: eclipse and partition resistance, DoS
resistance in message handling and resource accounting, and privacy of
transaction origin. Then relay correctness and liveness: blocks and
transactions propagate reliably and quickly, and nothing gets stuck.
Then interoperability with the rest of the network and with new
protocol features (BIPs) that other software depends on. Then bandwidth
and resource use, which node operators feel. Then connectivity across
network types and platforms.

Protocol changes with a specification and other implementations
waiting rank higher than local optimizations. Refactors count when they
retire a known hazard in message handling.
